claim: Imprecise-credence models represent belief as a set of probability functions with lower/upper envelopes; updating is member by member; the interval alone loses information.
schema_part: S0/O1 (an 'unknown' flag stored as low/high, not a point)
agent_test: Add a low/high field to claims at equal tokens; compare calibration of flagged-unknown vs point-only answers.
audit_note: SEP (Bradley) defines representor/credal set, lower and upper envelopes, updating by conditionalising each member, and says the summary functions lose information; Wikipedia agrees.

claim: Ellsberg-type preference for known-odds bets is common in humans (slightly more than half of subjects across 39 experiments, second-hand via Oechssler and Roomets; 55% of 708 subjects bet on a dominated risky urn). The Kuzmics 18 of 27 (66.67%) figure is the share of subjects who made a choice inconsistent with all classical (monotone) ambiguity models, not a plain preference rate.
agent_test: Not needed; background for why an 'unknown' flag is human-natural.
audit_note: Kuzmics et al. say 18 of 27 (66.67%) of SUBJECTS made an Ellsberg choice incompatible with all monotone (classical) ambiguity models, not a share of rules; other figures (slightly more than half across 39 experiments via Oechssler-Roomets, 55% of 708 in Jabarian-Lazarus) match.
claim_before_audit: Ellsberg-type preference for known-odds bets is common in humans (about half in 39 experiments, second-hand; 55% in a 708-person study bet on a dominated risky urn). The Kuzmics 18 of 27 figure is the share of rules inconsistent with all classical ambiguity models, not a plain preference rate.

claim: Ellsberg behaviour is heterogeneous and not fully explained by classical ambiguity models; some choices even violate dominance (55% prefer a risky act to a dominating ambiguous one) and revealed-preference consistency under uncertainty is about as good as under risk. In 154 subjects only 20 (13.0%) were perfectly rationalizable and none perfectly expected-utility rationalizable (Dembo 2026).
agent_test: Skip; theory dispute, no direct agent test.

claim: Dilation: observing evidence can widen an imprecise credence even when the evidence looks irrelevant (point 1/2 becomes [0,1]); this is a known cost of set-valued belief.
schema_part: G (guardrail: do not widen unknown flags on irrelevant evidence)
agent_test: Simulate: feed irrelevant evidence and check whether the agent's stated interval widens; count at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Belief inertia: a vacuous prior stays vacuous for every evidence, so the agent cannot learn; near-vacuous priors avoid it.
schema_part: O (never set an interval to the full [0,1]; use a weak prior)
agent_test: Compare intervals starting at [0,1] vs [0.05,0.95] on sequential evidence tasks.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Imprecise credences cause decision paralysis and incomparable options; Elga (2010) argues a sure-loss sequential bet pair forces sharp probabilities, while Levi's E-admissibility lets the agent refuse both bets.
schema_part: S/O (a tie-break rule when the interval spans the decision threshold)
agent_test: Give decisions whose interval straddles threshold; test tie-break rules (abstain, maximin, ask) at equal tokens.

claim: Verbalized LLM confidence is overconfident and a weak predictor of errors: GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% for vanilla verbalized confidence (Xiong et al.), and GPT-3.5 CoT verbalized confidence reaches only 54.8% AUROC on GSM8K.
agent_test: Measure ECE/AUROC of a verbalized low/high versus the point confidence on held-out QA.
audit_note: Xiong et al. report GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% for vanilla verbalized confidence, but the GSM8K AUROC of 54.8% is for GPT-3.5 with CoT verbalized confidence (Table 3), not GPT-4.
claim_before_audit: Verbalized LLM confidence is overconfident and a weak predictor of errors; GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% and GSM8K AUROC 54.8% for vanilla verbalized confidence.

claim: Sample consistency predicts failure far better than verbalized confidence on arithmetic (GSM8K AUROC 54.8 to 92.7), but the gain is mostly arithmetic: GPT-4 consistency AUROC on non-arithmetic tasks is 56 to 69, and with GPT-5 and gemini-2.5-pro on QA sample frequency is worse than a verbalized confidence.
agent_test: Build the interval from k=5 samples vs one verbalized interval at equal tokens; compare AUROC.

claim: Asking for several answers with probabilities before giving confidence cuts calibration error by a relative 50% or more on ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude 2.
agent_test: Add an 'enumerate alternatives then give low/high' step and measure ECE.

claim: LLMs rarely express their own uncertainty faithfully: faithfulness near chance (0.52-0.57 vanilla, best 0.63 GPT-4 and 0.70 Gemini Ultra).
agent_test: Check agreement between stated hedging words and sample-split on our agent.
audit_note: Yona et al. Table 1 gives vanilla cMFG 0.52-0.57, best 0.63 (GPT-4) and 0.70 (Gemini Ultra); Xiong corroborates poor verbalized-uncertainty quality.

claim: Ensemble-derived credal sets give abstain rules, but the earlier figure of 73-91% commit at 89-98% accuracy was not found in the full text. At a fixed 80% coverage CLLM+SCC reaches 99.0% (OpenBookQA), 71.5% (CoQA), 43.5% (TriviaQA), about equal to semantic entropy on the last two; the authors say it is not uniformly preferable.
schema_part: O (commit only if lower beats rival upper)
agent_test: Implement commit-if-lower>upper-of-rivals with 5 sampled answers; compare accuracy at fixed coverage.

claim: The LLM interval verbalized by prompting contains its own first-order point estimate only about 70% of the time (72.33% on AmbigQA); a containment constraint gives 100% at a cost of about 0.03 AUROC (0.7862 to 0.7554).
schema_part: G (consistency check: point must lie in interval)
agent_test: Check point-in-interval rate on our agent and add a containment rule.

claim: Reasoning LLMs show near-ceiling ambiguity aversion in the 50/50 versus unknown urn, and GPT and Llama choose the known urn in 100% of samples in one battery. Helzner (2026) does not test ambiguity aversion; Ellsberg prompts so far show both urns side by side.
agent_test: Run the two-urn item; but the effect on answer quality is unknown. Evidence is mixed: Claude 3.5 results were nulls (Helzner).

claim: Thinking tokens make LLM choices more consistent with expected utility.
agent_test: Low priority.

claim: Models struggle to detect and enumerate ambiguity: GPT-4 disambiguations are judged correct 32.0% of the time versus 89.7% crowdworker agreement with the dataset (AmbiEnt, 1,645 items); GPT-4 true/false accuracy on ambiguity is 63.0% vs 50% chance, other models 49.6-57.7%.
schema_part: S0 (ask or flag when input is underspecified)
agent_test: Test an 'ambiguity check' pre-step: does flagging then asking raise task accuracy at equal tokens.
audit_note: Liu et al. report GPT-4 true/false ambiguity accuracy of 63.0% vs 50% chance (other models 49.6-57.7%), so 57% is wrong for GPT-4; 32.0% correct disambiguations vs 89.7% crowdworker agreement and 1,645 items match; the other listed sources (Kirchhof, Tamkin, Hou) do not report these numbers.
claim_before_audit: Models struggle to detect and enumerate ambiguity: GPT-4 disambiguations correct 32% vs 90% for dataset (AmbiEnt, 1,645 items); ambiguity detection 57% vs 50% chance.

claim: Credal volume is a sound epistemic-uncertainty measure for 2 classes but loses continuity above 2 classes.
agent_test: Use per-label low/high not volume.

claim: No direct test was found of Keynes/Levi imprecise-credence prompting on LLM task accuracy at equal tokens; the credal-LLM papers (2025-2026) test white-box ensembles or elicitation, not a scaffold step. Closest test: a verbalized interval ties a plain verbalized confidence on AUROC (GPT-5 0.7713 vs 0.7756 on Non-AmbigQA), with no accuracy-at-equal-tokens test.
agent_test: The gap: run the equal-token test of an 'unknown' interval flag.

claim: Preference for the sample/ensemble interval over a stated number is consistent with Hullermeier and Waegeman's view that epistemic uncertainty needs set-valued representation.
agent_test: Background.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The comparative-ignorance effect: priced alone, known and unknown bets cost about the same ($17.94 vs $18.42, N=141); side by side $24.34 vs $14.85 (Fox and Tversky 1995). A close copy (N=97) found vague bags still priced far below clear bags alone (15.33 vs 5.42), so the effect disappears only partly.
schema_part: S0 (present one claim at a time to limit contrast penalty on vague claims; weak support)
agent_test: Show an LLM one claim at a time versus beside a precise rival and compare stated confidence; no such test exists.

claim: No source found tests, in LLMs, interval dilation on irrelevant evidence, tie-break rules for threshold-straddling intervals (abstain, maximin, ask, E-admissibility) by accuracy, a vacuous [0,1] flag, or independent replication of credal-set gains. Only LLM maximin/maximax alignment with own answers is reported.
agent_test: Run the four rules on a held-out set with a fixed token budget; check interval widening after distractor evidence.

claim: A verbalized interval has not been shown to beat a plain verbalized confidence: on QA with GPT-5 and gemini-2.5-pro the AUROCs are within about one SD in several cells (ProbInt 0.7753 vs Vanilla 0.7577 on Non-MAQA GPT-5; 0.7303 vs 0.6889 gemini). With a deterministic small model sampling gives AUROC 0.5 while the interval gives 0.6027.
schema_part: O (unknown flag as optional extra, not replacement)
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of final accuracy with and without the flag.
